---
title: "Glossary"
subtitle: "The terms the pages use, in plain words, with what the project actually ran."
---

## JSON

A plain-text way of writing a record so that every programming language can read it. A record is a list of named fields inside braces; a list is inside square brackets; text is in quotes; numbers and `null` (meaning "not given") stand alone. Trimen's entry, structured:

```json
{
  "surname": "TRIMEN",
  "given_names": "HENRY",
  "birth_year": null,
  "education": "M.B. (Lond.)",
  "honours": [{"award": "F.R.S.", "year": null}, {"award": "F.L.S.", "year": null}],
  "events": [
    {"position": "lecturer on botany", "place": "London", "year_start": 1867, "year_end": 1875},
    {"position": "senior assistant to department of botany", "place": "British Museum", "year_start": 1869, "year_end": 1879},
    {"position": "director Royal Botanical Gardens", "place": "Ceylon", "year_start": 1880, "year_end": null}
  ],
  "terminal": null
}
```

That is what the model is asked to return for each entry, what the Python validator checks against the source, and what the graph is built from. One object per line in a file is a corpus; a spreadsheet can be made from it in one command, and the reverse.

## The model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B

An open-weights language model released by Alibaba's Qwen team ([announcement](https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.6-35b-a3b)). The name says what it is: 35 billion parameters in total, of which about 3 billion are active for any one token ("A3B"), because it is a mixture-of-experts model: 256 small specialist sub-networks, of which eight plus one shared one are consulted per token. The effect is that it reads and writes at the speed and cost of a 3-billion-parameter model while carrying the knowledge of a 35-billion one. It can run in a "thinking" mode that reasons at length before answering; the project turned that off, because on long entries the reasoning ate the token budget and returned nothing.

**What it takes to run.** The whole model has to sit in GPU memory. At full precision that is about 70 GB, which means one datacentre card (an 80 GB A100 or H100) or four 24 GB consumer cards ([specifications and memory figures](https://apxml.com/models/qwen36-35b-a3b)). The project served it with vLLM, an open-source server that exposes the model through the same interface as the commercial APIs, so the same Python client talks to either. The overnight run used a university GPU box; the matching jobs used one H100 on a Compute Canada cluster, with vLLM started inside the batch job and the model's name on the server set to `qwen3-30b-a3b` ([job script](https://github.com/jburnford/col_matching/blob/main/nibi/qwen_b1_full.slurm)).

**If you do not have a cluster.** In rough order of effort:

1. **Rent the model by the token.** OpenRouter and similar brokers serve Qwen models through the same interface; you change one line, the server address, and pay per million tokens. The project's own bake-off script does exactly this ([`kg_bench_openrouter.py`](https://github.com/jburnford/col_matching/blob/main/kg_bench_openrouter.py)), pointing the same client at `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`. For 30,000 entries at a few hundred tokens each, the whole run is in the tens of millions of tokens, which at the prices such models list is dollars to tens of dollars; check the current price before you start. Free tiers exist and the script defaults to one, with the warning that free models drift on field names, which is why the prompt pins the keys.
2. **Rent a GPU by the hour.** Cloud GPU services rent an 80 GB card by the hour. An eight-hour run with the same vLLM command costs an evening's worth of hours; price it on the day.
3. **Run a compressed copy locally.** A 4-bit quantised version of the same model needs about 19 GB of memory, which fits a single 24 GB consumer card or a Mac with 32 GB of unified memory, under llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio. It is slower, perhaps an entry every 15 to 40 seconds rather than one a second, so a 30,000-entry corpus is days rather than a night, but the runner is resumable and it costs nothing after the hardware.
4. **Use a smaller sibling.** Qwen's 4 and 8 billion parameter dense models run on a laptop. Expect worse structuring; measure it against a reference set of 200 entries before trusting it, exactly as the project measured the 35B model against the in-session reference set.
5. **Use a commercial batch API.** The project's first fallback tier sent the entries the Python grammar refused to Gemini's batch endpoint at half the interactive price, overnight. Any provider's batch tier works the same way.
6. **Ask for an allocation.** Canadian researchers get Compute Canada (the Digital Research Alliance) time by application; in the United States, campus research computing or NSF ACCESS. The job script above is what an allocation lets you run.

Whichever route: keep the prompt, the validator and the post-normaliser the same, and run the 200-entry reference set first. The model is the swappable part.

## Other terms

**F-score.** One number summarising two: precision (of what the system found, how much was right) and recall (of what was there, how much the system found). An F-score of 0.6 means both are around six in ten. Trading Consequences scored 0.62 on commodities and 0.61 on places.

**QID.** A Wikidata identifier: the letter Q and a number, such as Q1800510 for Philip Wodehouse. Stable, language-neutral, and shared by everyone who grounds to Wikidata. A model's memory of one is not a lookup.

**Grounding.** Linking a name in your source to a shared identifier for the thing it names. The pages distinguish retrieving a candidate, reading its statements, and deciding the match.

**Vector search.** Search by meaning rather than by matching letters: the query and every item are turned into lists of numbers that place similar meanings near each other. "Walpole Island" by string finds an island in New Caledonia; by vector it finds the Ontario reserve. The WikidataMCP server offers this over Wikidata.

**MCP.** Model Context Protocol, a standard way of giving a model a tool, such as a search endpoint, that it can call and whose results come back as evidence rather than memory.

**vLLM.** An open-source server that runs an open model on a GPU and answers requests in the same format as the commercial APIs.

**Mixture of experts.** A model built from many small specialist networks, only a few of which run for each token, so it is cheap to run for its size.

**Quantisation.** Storing a model's numbers at lower precision (4 bits instead of 16) so it needs a quarter of the memory, at a small cost in quality.

**Reasoning mode.** A setting where the model writes out a chain of thought before answering. Helpful for hard questions; on this task it spent the whole budget thinking and produced no record.

**Regex.** A pattern language for matching text by shape ("capital letters, comma, names, a dash, then clauses ending in a year"). The project's first tier.

**Validator.** Python code that checks the model's output against the source and drops anything the source does not contain.

**Ledger.** An append-only file of decisions with reasons, such as the 917 merge groups, so that every decision can be revisited.

**Silver standard.** A set of cases labelled by hand after the fact, used to measure what the automated passes did. "Silver" because it is smaller and less exhaustively checked than a gold standard built in advance.

**Zero-false-positive gate.** A rule that accepts a link only when the evidence leaves no plausible alternative, and otherwise leaves it unlinked. It trades recall for precision, which is why a review queue exists.
